title: Trail Crew: East Bay Hills Maintenance
description: Swing a Pulaski and help keep miles of East Bay trails in shape. Monthly work parties tackle drainage, tread repair, and blowdown removal alongside park rangers.
fullDescription: East Bay Regional Park District's volunteer trail crew meets monthly at rotating trailheads across the Oakland and Castro Valley hills. Work parties focus on erosion control, water bar clearing, tread restoration, and invasive plant removal on heavily trafficked routes like Skyline National Trail and the Chabot Loop. Rangers provide all hand tools, gloves, and safety briefings. Volunteers should wear sturdy boots and bring water and lunch. This is physical outdoor work that trail runners, hikers, and mountain bikers especially appreciate.
nextSteps: Register at ebparks.org/volunteer. Earth Day volunteer events are scheduled for April 25, 2026 across multiple parks.

title: Presidio Native Plant Restoration
description: Restore native coastal scrub and dune habitat in the Presidio by removing invasive species and planting locally grown seedlings alongside park conservancy staff.
fullDescription: The Presidio Trust and Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy run one of the most ambitious urban habitat restoration programs in the country. Monthly volunteer stewardship days tackle French broom, Himalayan blackberry, and ice plant across the Presidio's 1,500 acres. Crews work in the dunes near Crissy Field, along the El Polin Loop, and on the Tennessee Hollow watershed. Conservancy staff lead every session, teaching volunteers to identify invasive vs. native plants as they work. All tools provided; wear layers and sun protection.
nextSteps: Register for an upcoming stewardship day at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Presidio Habitat Stewards meet Saturdays 9am–Noon and select Wednesdays. No advance training needed — new volunteers always welcome.

title: Ocean Beach Cleanup Crew
description: Join the Surfrider crew for regular cleanups at Ocean Beach, collecting trash and ghost gear before it washes out to sea.
fullDescription: Surfrider Foundation's SF Chapter holds regular beach cleanups at Ocean Beach, one of the longest urban beaches in the U.S. and a persistent litter hotspot. Volunteers fan out across designated sections, collecting single-use plastics, fishing line, cigarette butts, and occasional ghost gear. All bags, gloves, and pickup tools are provided at the trailhead parking lot. Data is logged for Surfrider's national ocean pollution tracking program. The event is family-friendly and takes about two hours. Stick around afterward — the crew usually grabs coffee at a nearby café.
nextSteps: Check the events calendar at sf.surfrider.org/calendar for upcoming cleanup dates. No pre-registration required — just show up.

title: Shorebird Nest Monitor
description: Monitor snowy plover and Forster's tern nesting sites along the East Bay shoreline from April through August, recording clutch counts and disturbance events.
fullDescription: Golden Gate Bird Alliance coordinates a network of volunteer nest monitors at Eastshore State Park and Albany Mudflat from early April through late August each year. Monitors walk assigned transects on weekend mornings, recording nest locations, egg and chick counts, and any human or predator disturbances using standardized data sheets. All protocols are taught at a free training workshop in late March. Binoculars and data sheets provided; volunteers should bring a spotting scope if they have one. This data directly informs habitat management decisions by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
nextSteps: Visit goldengatebirdalliance.org/volunteer to sign up. Monitors are asked to cover a minimum of 8 weekends across the April–August season.

title: Mt. Tamalpais Trail Steward
description: Help maintain the iconic trails of Mt. Tamalpais — clearing vegetation, building water bars, and protecting sensitive chaparral habitat used by hikers, bikers, and equestrians alike.
fullDescription: One Tam's trail stewardship program coordinates volunteer work parties across the 42,000-acre Tamalpais watershed. Monthly events are led by experienced crew leaders from the Marin County Parks, State Parks, and MMWD. Work typically involves brushing trail margins, installing erosion control structures, and clearing drainage on routes like the Dipsea Trail, Matt Davis Trail, and Coastal Trail. Volunteers are treated to sweeping views of the Marin coast and often encounter hawks, deer, and newts. Tools, gloves, and safety briefings provided. Boots and sun protection required.
nextSteps: Sign up for a work party at onetam.org/volunteer. Next confirmed stewardship day: April 4, 2026, 9am–2pm (Marin Water partnership event).

title: Elephant Seal Docent — Año Nuevo
description: Guide visitors through the elephant seal colony at Año Nuevo State Park, sharing natural history and ensuring the animals' safety during pupping and molting seasons.
fullDescription: Año Nuevo State Park hosts the largest mainland breeding colony of northern elephant seals in the world. Volunteer docents lead permitted tour groups across the dunes from December through May, interpreting seal behavior, life history, and conservation challenges. POST partners with California State Parks to train and coordinate the volunteer docent corps. Training is an intensive two-day workshop in late November. Docents are asked to commit to at least one weekend day per week during the season. A remarkable experience — you'll stand within feet of 2,000-pound bulls and newborn pups.
nextSteps: Apply by October 31 to attend the November training weekend. Submit your application at openspacetrust.org/volunteer.

title: Marine Mammal Care Volunteer
description: Assist veterinary staff with the feeding, cleaning, and monitoring of rescued harbor seals, California sea lions, and elephant seals at our Marin Headlands hospital.
fullDescription: The Marine Mammal Center is the world's largest marine mammal hospital, rescuing over 1,000 animals per year from Alaska to Baja California. Animal care volunteers are the heart of daily operations: they prepare fish diets, hand-feed pups, clean pools, collect behavioral observations, and assist vets during procedures. The commitment is serious — volunteers complete a multi-session training program and commit to the same 6-hour shift every week for a minimum of six months. In exchange, you'll develop deep knowledge of marine mammal medicine and ecology. Limited spots available; apply early.
nextSteps: Submit a volunteer application at marinemammalcenter.org/get-involved/volunteer/sausalito. Animal care positions require a minimum 6-month weekly commitment to the same shift.

title: Coyote Hills Wetland Restoration
description: Remove invasive pampas grass and salt cedar from ancient tule marshes at Coyote Hills, one of the Bay's best-preserved wetland complexes.
fullDescription: Coyote Hills Regional Park preserves 1,200 acres of Bay wetlands that have sustained human communities for over 2,000 years. Today, invasive plants threaten the tule, bulrush, and pickleweed communities that harbor rails, bitterns, and rare invertebrates. Monthly volunteer restoration days focus on cutting, bagging, and removing pampas grass clumps and salt cedar along marsh edges, followed by replanting with locally grown native sedges and rushes. Park naturalists provide plant ID training and lead discussions on wetland ecology. Tools and gloves provided; bring waders or rubber boots if you have them.
nextSteps: Register online at ebparks.org/get-involved/volunteer and select Coyote Hills work party dates. Events fill quickly — sign up at least two weeks in advance.

title: San Francisco Bay Water Quality Monitor
description: Collect water samples at designated Bay shoreline stations and enter data into a citizen science database tracking pollution, salinity, and nutrient levels over time.
fullDescription: Save the Bay's volunteer water quality monitoring program generates long-term data on Bay health at sites from Coyote Creek to San Pablo Bay. Trained monitors visit assigned stations monthly, collecting water samples, measuring dissolved oxygen and turbidity with field instruments, and recording observations about shoreline litter and wildlife activity. Data is submitted electronically and incorporated into Save the Bay's advocacy reports to the San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board. A two-hour online training is required before your first monitoring visit. Equipment is loaned to all active monitors.
nextSteps: Complete the online training at savesfbay.org/monitor and request an equipment kit. You'll be assigned a monitoring station within two weeks.

title: Peninsula Creek Restoration Crew
description: Restore native riparian vegetation along San Francisquito Creek in Palo Alto, creating habitat corridors for steelhead trout, great blue herons, and songbirds.
fullDescription: Grassroots Ecology focuses on restoring the creek and wetland ecosystems of the Santa Clara Valley. Their monthly creek restoration events along San Francisquito Creek in East Palo Alto and Palo Alto combine invasive removal (giant reed, English ivy, and Himalayan blackberry) with replanting of willows, sedges, and native forbs. Grassroots ecologists lead plant identification walks before each work session. The creek corridor provides critical habitat connectivity between the Bay and the Santa Cruz Mountains. All tools and native plants provided; youth volunteers age 12 and older are welcome with a parent or guardian.
nextSteps: Browse upcoming events and register at grassrootsecology.org/calendar. Multiple events scheduled in April 2026. Prior registration required for all events.

title: Bay Area Ridge Trail Builder
description: Work alongside trail professionals to build new sections of the 550-mile Bay Area Ridge Trail, connecting parklands from the North Bay to the South Bay.
fullDescription: The Bay Area Ridge Trail is a 550-mile vision trail linking over 75 parks along the ridgelines surrounding the Bay. The Ridge Trail Council coordinates volunteer construction crews working with professional trail builders to complete missing segments. Monthly work parties tackle tasks ranging from bench cutting on new tread to installing drainage structures and brushing sidehill sections. This is skilled, physical work. Crew leaders provide training in proper tool use and trail construction techniques. Volunteers must be able to hike to remote worksites with a 20 lb pack. Hard hats and tools provided.
nextSteps: Sign up for upcoming trail crew days at ridgetrail.org/volunteer. The annual Ridge Trail Service Day is November 7, 2026. New participants should read the Trail Crew FAQ before registering.

title: Outdoor Naturalist Education Docent
description: Lead school groups on guided nature walks through Tilden Regional Park, teaching students about Bay Area ecology, geology, and wildlife through hands-on outdoor activities.
fullDescription: The East Bay Regional Park District's Tilden Nature Area hosts over 20,000 school children each year through its environmental education program. Volunteer naturalist docents lead 90-minute walks for groups from kindergarten through 6th grade, using inquiry-based activities to explore topics like bird adaptations, plant communities, soil science, and creek ecosystems. Docents receive a 30-hour training course covering ecology content, facilitation skills, and child safety protocols. After training, volunteers commit to one weekday walk per week during the school year. Some of the most rewarding volunteering in the Bay Area — kids are endlessly surprising.
nextSteps: Apply for the next docent training cohort at ebparks.org/tilden-nature. Training runs September–November; applications due August 15.

title: Pelagic Bird Survey — Point Reyes
description: Join a research team conducting standardized seabird counts from the Point Reyes Headlands, contributing to long-term population data on murres, shearwaters, and alcids.
fullDescription: Golden Gate Bird Alliance coordinates quarterly pelagic bird surveys at Point Reyes Headlands in partnership with the Point Reyes Bird Observatory. Survey teams of 3–4 volunteers spend 6 hours at the headlands during peak migration windows, recording seabird species, numbers, and behaviors using standardized distance-sampling protocols. Common species include common murre, Brandt's cormorant, Cassin's auklet, and black-footed albatross. Volunteers receive a pre-survey training on identification cues and counting protocol. Spotting scope required (loaners available for first-timers). This is citizen science at its most impactful — the data informs federal fisheries management.
nextSteps: Visit goldengatebirdalliance.org/volunteer to sign up for the survey volunteer pool. Surveys are scheduled based on weather windows — flexibility is important.

title: Estuary Kayak Trash Patrol
description: Paddle kayaks through Islais Creek and Mission Creek channels to collect floating trash and document pollution sources in SF's urban waterways.
fullDescription: SF Rec & Parks partners with local kayak clubs to run monthly paddle cleanups in the city's urban creeks and marina channels. Volunteers use sit-on-top kayaks (provided) to access shallow areas unreachable by foot, scooping up floating plastic, fishing gear, and debris. The route covers Islais Creek from Cesar Chavez to Third Street and portions of Mission Creek near McCovey Cove. No kayaking experience required — a 15-minute orientation covers basic paddling and safety. Participants must be able to swim and are required to wear a PFD throughout. Data on trash quantity and type is submitted to the SF Estuary Institute.
nextSteps: Register at sfrecpark.org/volunteer at least one week before the event. Equipment is provided but space is limited to 12 participants.

title: Marin Open Space Trail Patrol
description: Hike or mountain bike designated trail patrol routes through Marin's open space preserves, providing visitor assistance and reporting maintenance needs and wildlife sightings.
fullDescription: The Marin County Open Space District manages 34 preserves covering more than 17,000 acres of open space across the county. Volunteer trail patrol ambassadors are the eyes and ears of these preserves. Patrols carry a radio and basic first aid kit, assist visitors with maps and regulations, document trail conditions (washouts, blowdown, erosion), and report wildlife observations including mountain lion sightings. Patrols are conducted solo or in pairs and are logged on a standard form submitted after each outing. Patrol volunteers attend a half-day orientation and commit to one patrol per month. Hiking patrols and mountain bike patrols both needed.
nextSteps: Apply at parks.marincounty.gov/discoverlearn/volunteer. Orientations are held quarterly in San Rafael.

title: Mount Tam Interpretive Trail Guide
description: Lead public interpretive hikes on Mt. Tamalpais, sharing natural and cultural history with visitors from around the world on one of the Bay Area's most beloved mountains.
fullDescription: One Tam's volunteer interpretive guide program trains passionate nature lovers to lead monthly public hikes on Mt. Tamalpais. Guides develop and lead 2–3 hour walks on routes like the Matt Davis Trail, Steep Ravine, and the East Peak summit circuit, weaving together stories of the mountain's ecology, Indigenous Miwok history, and conservation legacy. A 24-hour training program covers natural history content, public facilitation skills, and Leave No Trace principles. Guides are expected to lead at least one hike per month during the program season (April–October). An extraordinary way to deepen your own knowledge while sharing the mountain you love.
nextSteps: Apply for the spring guide training at onetam.org/volunteer. Training takes place over three weekends in April.

title: Bair Island Habitat Restoration
description: Remove invasive plants and restore native tidal marsh habitat at Bair Island, one of the largest undeveloped islands in San Francisco Bay.
fullDescription: Bair Island is a 1,600-acre complex of tidal marshes and mudflats within the Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge — and one of the most ecologically significant restoration sites in the Bay Area. Monthly volunteer workdays focus on pulling invasive plants and establishing native marsh vegetation under the guidance of POST and SF Bay Bird Observatory staff. The island provides critical habitat for the endangered salt marsh harvest mouse and Ridgway's rail, as well as thousands of migratory shorebirds. Workdays are best suited for ages 14 and older; all minors must be accompanied by an adult. No dogs. Rubber boots recommended.
nextSteps: Register at openspacetrust.org/volunteer. Next workday: April 11, 2026, 9am–12pm at Bair Island Public Parking, Redwood City.

title: EcoCenter Habitat Workparty — Heron's Head Park
description: Restore native coastal wetland habitat at Heron's Head Park, SF's only natural shoreline, alongside the EcoCenter team on the third Saturday of each month.
fullDescription: Heron's Head Park is a rare remnant of natural Bay shoreline tucked into the industrial southeastern waterfront of San Francisco. The SF Rec & Parks EcoCenter runs monthly habitat workparties here, removing invasive plants and establishing native species that support shorebirds, migratory waterfowl, and native pollinators. The park sits adjacent to the Islais Creek estuary and offers some of the best urban birding in the city. Volunteers work in small crews with experienced EcoCenter naturalists who provide tools, gloves, and ecological context for the restoration work. All ages and experience levels welcome.
nextSteps: Register at sfrecpark.org/volunteer. Workparties are held on the third Saturday of each month. Upcoming dates: April 18, May 16, and June 20, 2026.

title: Alcatraz Historic Gardens
description: Help restore the historic terraced gardens once tended by military families and penitentiary residents on Alcatraz Island, working alongside National Park Service and Conservancy garden staff.
fullDescription: Long before Alcatraz became a federal prison, it was home to gardens planted by military families and later maintained by inmates and their guards. Today, Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy volunteers help restore these historic terraced gardens, removing weeds, deadheading roses, and replanting heirloom varieties documented in historic photographs. Sessions run Wednesday and Thursday mornings and include the ferry ride to the island as part of the experience. All tools and gloves are provided; wear layered clothing and sturdy shoes for the uneven terrain.
nextSteps: Register for a Wednesday or Thursday session at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Ferry transportation from Pier 33 is arranged for registered garden volunteers.

title: Sutro Heights Historic Landscaping and Maintenance
description: Help maintain the historic landscaping and cultural resources at Sutro Heights Park, the clifftop remains of Adolph Sutro's 19th-century estate overlooking Ocean Beach.
fullDescription: Sutro Heights Park preserves the terraces, statuary, and gardens of Adolph Sutro's former clifftop estate above the Cliff House and Ocean Beach. Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy volunteers gather on the first and third Wednesday of each month to weed historic planting beds, prune hedges, and maintain pathways while learning about the park's Gilded Age history. No experience necessary — tools, gloves, and training are provided on site.
nextSteps: Register for an upcoming session at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Sessions run 9am–noon on the 1st and 3rd Wednesday of the month.

title: Presidio Tunnel Tops Stewards
description: Care for the native plant landscaping at Presidio Tunnel Tops, the park built over Doyle Drive connecting the Presidio to Crissy Field and the Golden Gate.
fullDescription: Presidio Tunnel Tops opened in 2022 as a 14-acre park connecting the main Presidio to Crissy Field, planted with native coastal scrub and grassland species. Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy stewardship volunteers help this young landscape establish by weeding, watering, and mulching planting beds during the April–September growing season. Sessions are held on the 2nd Tuesday, 4th Wednesday, and last Tuesday of each month. Tools and gloves provided — a great option for volunteers who want a shorter, family-friendly outdoor commitment with sweeping bay views.
nextSteps: Register at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Program runs seasonally April through September.

title: Ocean Beach Clean-ups
description: Join Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy's monthly clean-up to help keep Ocean Beach free of trash and marine debris.
fullDescription: Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy runs a monthly volunteer clean-up along Ocean Beach, one of the most heavily used stretches of national parkland shoreline in San Francisco. Volunteers walk assigned sections of beach collecting trash, cigarette butts, and washed-up debris using supplied buckets, gloves, and grabbers. Clean-ups meet on the first Saturday of the month; no registration or experience required, just show up ready to work outdoors.
nextSteps: Show up the first Saturday of the month, 10am–1pm. Check parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs for the meeting location, which varies along the beach.

title: Tamalpais Bee Lab
description: Assist One Tam's community science team surveying native bee populations across Mt. Tamalpais during the spring and summer flowering season.
fullDescription: The Tamalpais Bee Lab is a community science project tracking native bee diversity and abundance across the Tamalpais watershed as part of One Tam's broader effort to understand how the mountain's ecosystems are changing. Volunteers help set up pan traps and vane traps, net and photograph bees in the field, and sort and pin specimens back in the lab for identification. No entomology background needed — training is provided at the start of each season. Events run through the spring and summer months and tend to fill up quickly.
nextSteps: Email communityscience@onetam.org to join the volunteer list. Sign up early — sessions fill fast.

title: Marin Wildlife Watch
description: Help identify mammals captured on motion-activated wildlife cameras placed across Mt. Tamalpais as part of One Tam's long-term population monitoring.
fullDescription: Marin Wildlife Watch uses a network of motion-activated cameras placed across the Tamalpais watershed to track populations of bobcats, coyotes, deer, and other mammals over time. Volunteers join a seasonal cohort and use an online platform to review camera trap images and identify the species captured, contributing to a long-running dataset used by park scientists to understand wildlife trends. Training on the identification platform is provided; most work can be done remotely between occasional in-person camera checks.
nextSteps: Email communityscience@onetam.org to join the next fall/winter volunteer cohort.

title: Coastal Cleanup Day — MLK Regional Shoreline
description: Join Save The Bay and thousands of volunteers statewide for California's Coastal Cleanup Day, removing trash from the shoreline at MLK Regional Shoreline in Oakland.
fullDescription: Coastal Cleanup Day is California's largest volunteer event, bringing tens of thousands of people to shorelines statewide on a single September morning. Save The Bay hosts a cleanup at Martin Luther King Jr. Regional Shoreline in Oakland, where volunteers comb the marsh edges and trails for trash and plastic debris before it can wash into the Bay. Certified project leaders provide gloves, bags, and safety instruction; the event is family-friendly, though volunteers under 13 must be accompanied by a parent.
nextSteps: Register at savesfbay.org/event/coastal-cleanup-day-at-mlk-regional-shoreline-oakland-1oapyaq/. Event runs 9am–noon on Saturday, September 19, 2026.

title: Habitat Restoration at Eden Landing
description: Help restore former industrial salt ponds into tidal marsh habitat at Eden Landing Ecological Reserve in Hayward, removing invasive mustard alongside Save The Bay's restoration team.
fullDescription: Eden Landing Ecological Reserve is part of the South Bay Salt Pond Restoration Project, the largest tidal wetland restoration effort on the West Coast. Save The Bay volunteers help convert former commercial salt ponds back into functioning marsh by removing invasive mustard and other weeds and planting native marsh vegetation that will support shorebirds, fish, and endangered species like the salt marsh harvest mouse. Certified project leaders lead the workday and provide all tools, gloves, and safety training; no experience necessary.
nextSteps: Register at savesfbay.org/event/habitat-restoration-at-eden-landing-hayward-1jxwyay/. Event runs 9am–noon on Saturday, October 3, 2026.

title: Tennessee Valley Tuesday Stewards
description: Get your hands dirty restoring and protecting native plant communities at Tennessee Valley, one of the Marin Headlands' most scenic canyons.
fullDescription: Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy's Tennessee Valley Tuesday Stewards meet on the 3rd and 5th Tuesdays of the month from 10am to 2pm at rotating sites within Tennessee Valley. Work focuses on removing invasive weeds and restoring native plant communities along the valley's grasslands and creek corridor. Conservancy staff lead every session and provide tools, gloves, and plant ID guidance; no experience necessary.
nextSteps: Register for an upcoming session at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Sessions run 10am–2pm on the 3rd and 5th Tuesday of the month.

title: Presidio Forest Stewards
description: Help tend the health of the Presidio's historic forests while repairing and maintaining the trails that run through them.
fullDescription: The Presidio's forested ridgelines are a legacy of the Army's 19th-century tree-planting campaign, and today they need active stewardship to stay healthy. Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy's Presidio Forest Stewards meet Friday mornings from 9am to noon to thin overcrowded stands, clear deadfall, and repair trail tread and drainage through the forest. Tools and training provided on site; wear sturdy boots.
nextSteps: Register for a Friday session at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs.

title: Presidio Nursery
description: Learn to grow native plants from seed at the Presidio Nursery, which supplies the seedlings used in restoration projects across the park.
fullDescription: The Presidio Nursery propagates thousands of native plants each year for restoration sites throughout the Presidio. Volunteers help with seed collection and cleaning, transplanting, watering, and general nursery upkeep. A weekly Wednesday shift is available for volunteers who want a regular commitment, and a drop-in open nursery day runs one Saturday a month for anyone who wants to try it without a standing commitment. No experience required — training happens on the job.
nextSteps: Register at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs and choose a Wednesday shift or the monthly open Saturday.

title: Black Point Historic Gardens
description: Help restore the long-neglected historic gardens of East Black Point at Fort Mason, once part of a 19th-century Army post's grounds.
fullDescription: East Black Point's gardens, overlooking the Bay at Fort Mason, fell into disrepair for decades before Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy volunteers began restoring them. Sessions run Thursday afternoons (2–5pm), Friday mornings (9am–noon), and the first Saturday of the month (10am–1pm), and involve weeding, pruning, and replanting historic garden beds. All tools and gloves provided.
nextSteps: Register for a session at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs.

title: Fort Mason Historic Landscaping and Maintenance
description: Help maintain the historic landscapes and cultural resources of Upper Fort Mason, a former Army post overlooking San Francisco Bay.
fullDescription: Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy volunteers gather Tuesday mornings from 9am to noon at Upper Fort Mason to weed planting beds, prune shrubs, and maintain pathways while learning about the site's military history. No experience necessary — tools, gloves, and training provided on site.
nextSteps: Register for a Tuesday session at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs.

title: Marin Headlands Nursery
description: Grow native plants from seed at the Marin Headlands Nursery to help preserve and restore the Headlands' coastal grasslands and scrub.
fullDescription: The Marin Headlands Nursery grows the native plant stock used in restoration projects across the Headlands. Volunteers help with seed collection, transplanting, watering, and nursery upkeep. A weekly Wednesday shift suits volunteers who want a standing commitment; a drop-in open nursery day runs one Saturday a month for anyone who wants to try it first. No experience necessary.
nextSteps: Register at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs and choose a Wednesday shift or the monthly open Saturday.

title: Habitat Restoration Team
description: Help restore and monitor critical natural areas from the Marin Headlands to Bolinas Ridge, removing invasive plants and protecting sensitive habitat alongside Conservancy staff.
fullDescription: Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy's Habitat Restoration Team tackles invasive weed removal, native plant establishment, and habitat monitoring across sites spanning the Marin Headlands to Bolinas Ridge. Crews meet Sunday mornings at rotating trailheads, working under the guidance of Conservancy restoration staff. No experience necessary — tools, gloves, and training are provided on site.
nextSteps: Register for an upcoming Sunday session at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Sessions run 9:30am–2:30pm.

title: Invasive Plant Patrol
description: Hike Marin's backcountry with a mission — help find and remove new infestations of invasive weeds before they can spread across the Headlands and beyond.
fullDescription: The Invasive Plant Patrol combines hiking with early-detection weed control, searching remote corners of the Marin Headlands and surrounding open space for newly established invasive plants. Volunteers cover ground that scheduled restoration crews rarely reach, pulling small infestations before they take hold. Conservancy staff lead every outing and provide plant ID training, tools, and gloves. A good fit for volunteers who enjoy off-trail hiking as much as habitat work.
nextSteps: Register for a Wednesday outing at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Sessions run 10am–2:30pm.

title: San Francisco Habitat Stewards
description: Help restore and preserve the natural areas of Fort Funston, Lands End, and the Presidio, removing invasive plants and creating habitat corridors for coastal wildlife.
fullDescription: Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy's San Francisco Habitat Stewards work across three of the city's wildest national park sites — Fort Funston, Lands End, and the Presidio — removing invasive species and restoring native coastal scrub and dune habitat. Sessions rotate between a Wednesday morning shift and a Thursday afternoon shift. Conservancy staff lead every outing; no experience necessary, and all tools and gloves are provided.
nextSteps: Registration required — sign up at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Sessions run Wednesdays 9am–Noon and Thursdays 1–4pm.

title: Golden Gate Historic Landscaping and Maintenance
description: Help protect and beautify the historic landscapes and cultural resources along the Golden Gate, from Lands End and Baker Beach to Crissy Field and Ocean Beach.
fullDescription: This Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy program cares for the historic landscaping and cultural resources found across the park's western shoreline sites, including Lands End, Crissy Field, Baker Beach, and Ocean Beach. Thursday volunteer sessions rotate among these locations, focusing on weeding, pruning, and general landscape upkeep around historic structures and overlooks. Tools, gloves, and training provided; no experience necessary.
nextSteps: Register for a Thursday session at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. Sessions run 10am–1pm.

title: Roving Ranger — Pop-Up Trailhead Host
description: Meet hikers and visitors at Mt. Tamalpais trailheads, sharing trip-planning tips and stewardship messages as part of One Tam's mobile "Roving Ranger" outreach.
fullDescription: One Tam's Roving Ranger program sets up pop-up information stations at rotating trailheads across the Tamalpais watershed to greet visitors before they head out. Volunteers answer questions about routes and conditions, share tips for a safe and low-impact visit, and help promote stewardship of the mountain's trails and habitat. Shifts are offered on both weekdays and weekends with a flexible schedule, making this a good fit for volunteers who enjoy people-facing outdoor work without a fixed weekly commitment.
nextSteps: Email mstafford@onetam.org to ask about upcoming Roving Ranger trailhead shifts on Mt. Tamalpais.
